title: I finally figured out what's been causing most of my biggest losses... and it wasn't my strategy.
author: Electronic_Tea_2948
selftext:
I went through my trading journal over the weekend because I couldn't understand why some weeks were so much worse than others.

What surprised me was that my biggest losses almost never came from my first bad trade. They came from the one right after it. I'd lose on a perfectly valid setup, get frustrated, convince myself the next trade \*had\* to work, increase my size, and completely ignore my own rules. Looking back, revenge trading has probably cost me more money than bad analysis ever has. I'm trying to build rules around this now, but I'm curious...   
Has anyone actually found a way to stop themselves after taking a frustrating loss?

comments.author: Jollyfroggy
comments.body:
100% very common.

This is the sunk cost phalacy / phenomenon.


You buy something, it's yours now you value it more than what you paid.

Weirdly, there are cases where it's not wrong and some good reasons that humans do this and it's to do with caveman risk.

You spend some time collecting something, say fruit. The fruit is good. It took you X effort to get the fruit, but as the fruit is not damaged or mouldy, you value it higher than the effort it took to get it.

Another one most people will be familiar with are cars. You have a car, it's 20 years old and worth 3k on the market, but it's your car and you know it, so you personally value it higher than 3k.

Problem is, our brains tend to apply this to abstract stuff too. Shares are one.

You do your research, buy something, it goes down, but you're already bought in, so you buy more!


The solution is to take the emotion out of it.

Your assets are your assets, at any point in time they are worth what they are worth, not what you paid for them, this is one of the reasons I hate the averaging down rhetoric.

You should buy something if you think it will go up in price. Specifically you should buy the thing that will make you the most money or the best result according to your strategy.

I think the key thing is managing ego.
If a stock goes down when you thought it would go up. Why, what changed, what were your assumptions from your research, are they still valid?
If yes, sure maybe buy more, but at the same time, is there something better?


I also ran a bunch of backtests and in general they found that the best strategy was: fill portfoli, leave it for 6 months, reassess and rebalance, ignoring all previous purchases.

The only exception were a few major crashes, which, eh, too much to go into, but there were a few times it was better to pull out than leave in.

comments.author: Investinginevtol
comments.body: No room for sentiment in trading.  Every so often sell everything, then wait a day and decide if you want to buy it back

comments.author: ochimaru420
comments.body: Trade timeout. Your strategy may be have edge but the market is influenced by 1000 things.  A logical uptrend can sideswiped by an unpredictable real world factor completely invalidating your strategy.  A timeout let's the market settle.  Instead do a deep dive on the data, figure out why it lost.  If it's news based it may take time before you learn. So many times i experience an unexpected crash and later learn it was due to some political, international or corporate news shock.

comments.author: egamemnon
comments.body:
I've been hit coincidentally just recently. Just now, I've kind of solved a problem. I restructured the process because everything looked perfect, but there were the small trades, the micro scalp. It's purely my fault.

The steps were:  
1. Position sizing and spread friction repairs, like halting all of the stupid micro tickets because of the round tripography.  
2. New ticket minimum, which is $250.  
3. Friction coverage rule: a requirement of a minimum of 5:1 expected profit-to-spread ratio prior to entry.  
4. The capital and asset constraints  
5. Liquidity filtering.  
6. Cash risk ceiling.  
7. : Dual stream telemetry and log purification. More like ritual sacrifice.

If we're on the same page, then we're on the same page.

comments.author: TradersToolChest
comments.body: One of the things that helped me was making the rule physical: after any loss, close the platform and walk away for at least 15 minutes before I'm allowed to look at another setup. That gap forces you to decide if the next trade is a real setup or just frustration looking for a win back.

comments.author: mushykindofbrick
comments.body: Why would revenge trading lose you more money than a random strategy? It's still random trading, so it should be 50/50 before fees. On average, doing revenge trades you should only lose the fees for those trades. If it's more you just had bad luck. Or more likely, your strategy would not work even without the revenge trades.
